## Installing kintera (`pip install kintera` or a source build) {#sec-ch01-install}

### Summary

kintera is a C++ library with a Python package on top, and both are needed to run it from Python. There are two
routes. The PyPI package installs a released build in one command. A source build compiles the commit you check out,
which is the only way to run exactly the code this report describes. At the time of writing the newest PyPI release
is older than the code pin (see Limits).

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Get a working `import kintera`.

**Data.** Python 3.10 or later, `torch` 2.10.0, `pyharp` 2.2.0 or later; for a source build also a C++17 compiler,
CMake and the NetCDF C library.

**Placement.** Before @sec-ch01-quick-start.

**Activation.** Either route; the source build follows the README of the pinned commit.

**Guarantee / limits.** Both routes were run for this chapter; see the Tests layer.

**Evidence.** Run records in the Tests layer.
:::

The requirements are those the README states: a C++17 compiler (it names GCC 9 or later), CMake 3.18 or later,
Python 3.10 or later, and the NetCDF C library ({{< code README.md >}}). The package version is not written in any
file; it comes from the git tags at build time (@sec-ch11-version).

### Derivation

No derivation: this section is an installation procedure.

### Numerical method

No numerical method and no figure: this section is an installation procedure. The two routes are these.

**PyPI.** In a fresh virtual environment:

```bash
pip install kintera
```

This also installs `torch`, `pyharp` and `pydisort` as dependencies.

**Source build.** The steps of the README ({{< code README.md >}}), with the checkout at the commit to be run:

```bash
pip install numpy 'torch==2.10.0' 'pyharp>=2.2.0'
git clone https://github.com/chengcli/kintera.git
cd kintera
git checkout <commit>
cmake -B build
cmake --build build --parallel
pip install .
```

`cmake -B build` finds `torch` and the `pydisort` and `pyharp` packages through the active Python interpreter, so it
must run in the environment where step 1 installed them. CUDA is used only when CMake finds a CUDA compiler
(@sec-ch12-build).

### Code

| what | code link | symbol | switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| install instructions | {{< code README.md >}} | `README.md` | always |
| top-level build | {{< code CMakeLists.txt >}} | `find_package(Disort)` | always |
| Python package build | {{< code setup.py >}} | `setup.py` | `pip install .` |
| version and dependencies | {{< code pyproject.toml >}} | `pyproject.toml` | always |

: Code map of installation. {#tbl-ch01-install-code}

1. `CMakeLists.txt` requires `Torch`, `Disort` and `Harp` before it adds the sources ({{< code CMakeLists.txt >}}).
2. `pip install .` builds the Python extension through `setup.py` and installs the package.
3. On import, the package adds its own `data` directory to the resource search path (@sec-ch11-resources).

Both routes were run in fresh virtual environments, CPU only. The source build at the pin installed kintera 2.6.5;
`pip install kintera` installed kintera 2.6.4.[^ch01-build][^ch01-pip] The CUDA path was not built for this chapter.

### Limits

- The newest PyPI release, 2.6.4, is older than the code pin, which is tagged 2.6.5. Code described in this report
  may differ from what `pip install kintera` provides; for exact agreement build from source at the pin.
- With the CPU-only `torch` build, `pyharp` and `pydisort` 2.7.6 and 1.8.13 fail to import (they look for
  `libtorch_cuda.so`), and the source build's CMake step then stops in `FindDisort.cmake`. Installing `torch==2.10.0`
  from PyPI, as the README writes it, avoids this; the run record notes the failed first attempt.[^ch01-build]
- The README names GCC 9 as the minimum; the run used GCC 13.3.1. Older compilers were not tried.
- Only Linux x86-64 with Python 3.11 was tried.
